name: Indigenous peoples of Siberia
summary: The many peoples of Siberia, such as the Evenks and other Tungusic peoples, the Yakuts (Sakha), Chukchi, Nenets and Khanty, who lived by hunting, fishing and reindeer herding long before Russian expansion from the 1580s.

knownFor.label: Reindeer herding
knownFor.note: Herding and riding reindeer across the taiga and tundra.

knownFor.label: Shamanism
knownFor.note: The word “shaman” comes from the Evenki language.

knownFor.label: Chum (tent)
knownFor.note: A cone-shaped tent of poles and reindeer hides.

location.value: Siberia: from the Ural Mountains to the Pacific and from the Arctic Ocean to Mongolia.

terrain.value: Taiga forest, tundra, great rivers (Ob, Yenisei, Lena) and mountains.

resources.value: Reindeer, fish, fur animals (sable), sea mammals on the coasts.

disasters.value: Extreme cold and hunger in bad years.

population.value: About 160,000 at the start of the 17th century; about 1.6 million people belonged to Indigenous peoples of Siberia in the 2021 census.
population.source: Wikipedia: Indigenous peoples of Siberia (checked 9 Nov 2026)

disease.value: Diseases such as smallpox, together with massacres, killed many after the Russian conquest; in Kamchatka (annexed 1697) most of the Itelmen and Koryaks died.
disease.source: Wikipedia: Indigenous peoples of Siberia (checked 9 Nov 2026)

migration.value: Turkic Yakuts moved north into the Lena valley (about 13th–15th centuries).

economicBase.value: Hunting, fishing, gathering and reindeer herding; horses and cattle among the Yakuts.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade in furs with Chinese, Mongol and later Russian traders.

moneyAndTax.value: Russians demanded fur tribute (yasak) from the 17th century.

governmentType.value: No states (except the Khanate of Sibir in the west); clans and family groups.

keyRulers.value: No recorded rulers in most groups.

stability.value: Groups moved with herds and seasons.

armyAndTech.value: Bows, spears; Chukchi armour of hardened leather strengthened with wood and bone.
armyAndTech.source: Wikipedia: Indigenous peoples of Siberia (checked 9 Nov 2026)

majorWars.value: Resisted Russian conquest, especially the Chukchi: after Russian campaigns in 1730–31 and 1744–47, they killed the Russian commander Pavlutsky (1747).
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Indigenous peoples of Siberia (checked 9 Nov 2026)

territoryChange.value: Lost control of land to the Russian state.

alliancesRivals.value: Traded with Mongols, Manchus, Chinese and Russians.

inventions.value: Reindeer sleds, fur clothing, birch-bark boats.

openness.value: Adopted metal tools and later Christianity in parts.

communicationTransport.value: Reindeer and dog sleds in winter, boats on the great rivers in summer, skis for hunting.

religion.value: Shamanism and animal spirits; some Buddhism (Buryats) and Orthodox Christianity later.

languageWriting.value: Many language families: Uralic, Tungusic, Turkic, Chukotko-Kamchatkan and isolates.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Indigenous peoples of Siberia (checked 9 Nov 2026)

artsArchitecture.value: Beadwork, embroidery, epic songs (the Yakut olonkho).

dailyLife.value: Conical tents of reindeer hide or birch bark (chum), and log or earth houses in winter; meals of reindeer meat, fish and berries.

colonisation.value: Conquered by the Russian state from the late 16th century (from the 1580s) to the 19th century.
colonisation.source: Wikipedia: Indigenous peoples of Siberia (checked 9 Nov 2026)

riseSignals.value: Adapted to some of the harshest climates on Earth.

declineSignals.value: Russian conquest, the fur trade and disease.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Indigenous peoples of Siberia (checked 9 Nov 2026)

outcome.value: Many Siberian peoples live in Russia today, some in their own republics (such as Sakha).
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Indigenous peoples of Siberia (checked 9 Nov 2026)

sources.value: Wikipedia: Indigenous peoples of Siberia; Forsyth, A History of the Peoples of Siberia (1992).

overallCertainty.value: Mostly known from archaeology and Russian records; early figures are estimates.
